name: Word Odd One Out
blurb: Four words belong together. Find the one that does not.
childIntro: Look at all five words. Four of them belong in one group. Find the one that does not fit.
howItWorks: Five words are given and the child marks the one that does not belong. It runs at OLSAT levels D through G. The odd word is usually connected to the group in some other way, so a child who stops at the first plausible category gets it wrong.
parentTip: The single most useful habit: make the category as narrow as possible. Chair, sofa, recliner, table, bench are all furniture, so furniture is not the rule. Furniture you sit on is. If more than one word fits your rule, the rule is too broad.

questions.explanation: A chair, a sofa, a bench and a stool are all furniture you sit on. A table is furniture, but you do not sit on it.
questions.strategy: Furniture is too broad. Furniture you sit on is the real rule.

questions.explanation: Gold, silver, bronze and iron are metals. A medal is made from metal but is not a metal itself. Olympic medals make you want to pick iron, which is the trap.
questions.strategy: Watch for a word that pulls you toward the wrong group by association.

questions.explanation: Whisper, shout, mumble and yell are all ways of making sound with your voice. Listening is taking sound in, not putting it out.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction the action goes: in or out.

questions.explanation: Predict, forecast, foresee and anticipate all mean to say what will happen in the future. Observe is about what is happening now.
questions.strategy: When words are close in meaning, check WHEN they point: past, present or future.

questions.explanation: An island, a peninsula, a cape and an isthmus are all pieces of land in or beside water. An ocean is the water itself.
questions.strategy: Land and water are two different groups. Sort them before you choose.

questions.explanation: A nurse, a pilot, a plumber and an electrician are all jobs. A hospital is a place.
questions.strategy: Jobs, places and things are different kinds of word. Match kind to kind.

questions.explanation: A second, a minute, an hour and a day are all units used to measure time. Time is the thing being measured, not a unit of it.
questions.strategy: Never pick the name of the group. That is the most common wrong answer.

questions.explanation: A beetle, an ant, a bee and a moth are insects with six legs. A spider has eight legs and is not an insect.
questions.strategy: Counting legs settles insect questions every time.

questions.explanation: A trunk, a branch, a root and a leaf are all parts of a tree. The tree is the whole thing, not a part.
questions.strategy: Part and whole groups have the same trap as category groups. Do not pick the whole.

questions.explanation: Count the sides: a triangle has three, a pentagon five, a heptagon seven, a nonagon nine. All odd. A rectangle has four, which is even.
questions.strategy: When the words are all shapes, count the sides and look for odd and even.

questions.explanation: A carrot, a potato, an onion and a pea are vegetables. An apple is a fruit.
questions.strategy: Fruit and vegetables are different groups even though both are food.

questions.explanation: Hearing, listening, overhearing and eavesdropping are all ways of taking sound in. Shouting puts sound out.
questions.strategy: Ask which way the action goes: in or out.

questions.explanation: A hammer, a saw, a drill and a wrench are all tools. A nurse is a person.
questions.strategy: Sort the words by kind first: people, tools, places, things.

questions.explanation: A lake, a pond, a puddle and a reservoir are all still water sitting in one place. A river flows from one place to another.
questions.strategy: Look for a smaller difference when everything shares the obvious feature.

questions.explanation: A kitchen, a bedroom, a bathroom and a hallway are all rooms in a house. A library is a whole building.
questions.strategy: Check the scale. A room and a building are different sizes of thing.

questions.explanation: Tomorrow, later, soon and next week all point to the future. Yesterday points to the past.
questions.strategy: Time words split into past, present and future. Sort them first.

questions.explanation: Count the sides: a triangle has three, a pentagon five, a heptagon seven, a nonagon nine. All odd. A square has four, which is even.
questions.strategy: When all the words are shapes, count the sides and check odd or even.

questions.explanation: Silk, wool, leather and fur all come from animals. Cotton comes from a plant.
questions.strategy: Ask where each one comes from, not just what it is used for.

questions.explanation: A shark, a tuna, a cod and a salmon are fish, which breathe with gills. A whale is a mammal and breathes air.
questions.strategy: Living in the sea is not the same as being a fish.

questions.explanation: A meter measures length, a liter volume, a gram weight and a degree temperature. All four measure something physical about an object. A minute measures time.
questions.strategy: Group units by what they measure, not by how big they are.

questions.explanation: A hammer, a screwdriver, pliers and a chisel are all tools for building. A guitar is a musical instrument.
questions.strategy: Name the group in words. Tools for building, not just things you hold.

questions.explanation: Oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and helium are all gases. Copper is a solid metal.
questions.strategy: Solid, liquid and gas is a quick way to split a list.

questions.explanation: The Nile, the Amazon, the Danube and the Thames are all named rivers. Lake is a general word, not the name of anything.
questions.strategy: A general word among four names is almost always the odd one out.

questions.explanation: Predicting, forecasting, anticipating and expecting all look forward. Remembering looks back.
questions.strategy: When words are close in meaning, check WHEN they point.

questions.explanation: Hail, sleet, snow and rain are all water falling from the sky. Lightning is electricity.
questions.strategy: Ask what each one is made of, not just where it comes from.

questions.explanation: A violin, a cello, a viola and a harp are all instruments with strings. An orchestra is the group that plays them.
questions.strategy: Never pick the group. Pick a member of it, or spot the group as the odd one.

questions.explanation: An antidote, medicine, a cure and a remedy all make you better. Venom makes you ill.
questions.strategy: Look at the effect. Helping and harming are opposite groups.

questions.explanation: A cube, a sphere, a pyramid and a cylinder are all solid shapes you could hold. A circle is flat.
questions.strategy: Flat and solid shapes are two different families.

questions.explanation: Granite, limestone, marble and sandstone are all named kinds of rock. A pebble is a small piece of rock of any kind, so it describes the size, not the type.
questions.strategy: Check whether a word names a type or a size.

questions.explanation: Honesty, kindness, bravery and patience are all naming words for qualities. Honest is a describing word.
questions.strategy: Words can be sorted by their job in a sentence, not only by meaning.
